papers.title_in_file: Quantum Computing Education for Computer Science Students: Bridging the Gap with Layered Learning and Intuitive Analogies
papers.what_it_is: A proposal paper for a layered, analogy-based quantum computing curriculum for computer science students, with no student evaluation.

assertions.value: The authors propose a layered (scaffolded) learning approach that teaches quantum computing to computer science students from classical computing concepts and analogies, and state that it differs from existing approaches that require physics prerequisites or ground the foundations in linear algebra.
quotes: We posit that to teach quantum computing effectively to computer science students without a background in quantum mechanics, we need a layered (scaffolded) approach that builds on the existing knowledge of classical computing
This differs from existing approaches which either require advanced pre-requisites in physics or ground their foundations in linear algebra [3].
assertions.certainty_reason: The authors posit the approach; the paper presents no test of it.
assertions.reader_inference: The proposal is untested in the paper itself.

assertions.value: The authors state that comprehensive assessments to measure the effectiveness of the proposed teaching methodology are still needed, and list them as future work.
quotes: It is also necessary to conduct comprehensive assessments and evaluations to measure the effectiveness of the proposed teaching methodologies.
assertions.certainty_reason: Sec. V.A states that effectiveness has not yet been measured.

assertions.value: The authors report, citing Didis, that in a study of analogy use in teaching introductory quantum theory there was no systematic use of analogies, with 90% of them developed spontaneously.
quotes: Interestingly, there was no systematic use of analogies, with 90% of them being developed spontaneously [4].
assertions.certainty_reason: The result is cited from reference [4], not produced by this paper.

papers.title_in_file: HOPSO: A Robust Classical Optimizer for VQE
papers.what_it_is: A simulation study of a periodic-aware harmonic-oscillator particle swarm optimizer (HOPSO) for VQE on hydrogen and lithium hydride Hamiltonians.

assertions.value: The authors report that in noiseless simulations on the smaller hydrogen molecule COBYLA outperformed the other methods, and that with simulated shot noise of 1000 shots HOPSO showed the best overall performance among the population-based optimizers.
quotes: Surprisingly, COBYLA outperformed the other methods in this setting
Specifically, we set the number of shots to 1000 in Qiskit
Among them, HOPSO demonstrated the best overall performance.
assertions.certainty_reason: Results are from simulations of one molecule, reported in figures (Fig. 4, Fig. 5).
assertions.reader_inference: The abstract wording that HOPSO is more robust in all situations is stronger than the noiseless hydrogen result, where COBYLA won.

assertions.value: The authors report that on the larger lithium hydride system HOPSO and PSO both reached tight clusters near the known ground state energy, with HOPSO marginally more accurate and stable, and that under shot noise HOPSO kept energy estimates close to the true ground state with minimal variance while DE performed worst.
quotes: HOPSO and PSO both achieved tight clusters near the known ground state energy of LiH, with HOPSO exhibiting marginally higher accuracy and stability.
HOPSO maintained strong performance despite the presence of noise, consistently producing energy estimates close to the true ground state with minimal variance.
assertions.certainty_reason: Simulation results shown in Fig. 7 and Fig. 8; no hardware run.

assertions.value: The authors state that the lithium hydride problem was reduced to an 8-qubit Hamiltonian with 80 parameters, that each optimizer was given 800,000 function evaluations per run, that COBYLA was excluded from this system because it is sequential, and that the core-hour budget for the LiH study exceeded 50,000.
quotes: yielding an 8-qubit effective representation while preserving key energy characteristics.
To tackle this high-dimensional optimization space (80 parameters)
Each optimizer was allowed 800,000 function evaluations per run, corresponding to 10,000 iterations over 80 particles. COBYLA was excluded because of its inherently sequential structure
The estimated core-hour budget for the entire LiH study exceeded 50,000
assertions.certainty_reason: Sec. 5 states the paper's own setup and resource use.
assertions.reader_inference: The LiH comparison covers only HOPSO, PSO and DE; COBYLA, the winner on the hydrogen system, was not run.

assertions.value: The authors list integration with error mitigation and ansatz adaptation on real quantum hardware as future work; the reported experiments are simulations.
quotes: its integration with error mitigation and ansatz adaptation protocols on real quantum hardware.
assertions.certainty_reason: Sec. 6 names real hardware as future work.

papers.title_in_file: Exponential quantum advantages in learning quantum observables from classical data
papers.what_it_is: A learning-theory paper that proves a quantum learning advantage for learning quantum observables from classical measured-out data, under a complexity assumption.

assertions.value: The paper proves quantum learning advantages for learning quantum observables from classical (measured out) data, for linear combinations of Pauli strings and for unitarily parametrized observables, basing the classical hardness results on the assumption that BQP hard processes cannot be simulated by polynomial-size classical circuits.
quotes: we prove quantum advantages for the physically relevant task of learning quantum observables from classical (measured out) data.
we base our classical hardness results on the weaker assumption that BQP hard processes cannot be simulated by polynomial-size classical circuits
assertions.certainty_reason: Theorems 1 to 4 (Sec. IV) and Theorem 5 with Corollary 1 (Sec. V), conditional on the stated assumption.
assertions.reader_inference: The result is a separation under a complexity assumption for constructed tasks; it does not show an advantage on a practical dataset.

assertions.value: The paper states that it also examines the Hamiltonian learning problem, for which identifying the target function is demonstrated to be classically easy, so no advantage arises there.
assertions.anchor: Sec. I and Table I, p.2-3
quotes: We also examine the Hamiltonian learning problem where the identification of the target function is demonstrated to be classically easy.
assertions.certainty_reason: Stated in the contributions list and Table I; treated in Sec. V.B.

assertions.value: The authors state that their framework requires the Hamiltonian to be chosen randomly and the learner to be informed afterwards which Hamiltonian was selected.
quotes: we require both that the Hamiltonian is chosen randomly and that we are later informed about which Hamiltonian was selected
assertions.certainty_reason: Sec. VI states the data-distribution assumption of the framework.

assertions.value: The authors state that the hardness of the physical Hamiltonian examples beyond the listed BQP-complete families remains purely conjectural, and that their proof uses a contrived Kitaev Hamiltonian for technical simplicity.
quotes: While in our proof we deal with the contrived Kitaev Hamiltonian, this is only for technical simplicity.
We acknowledge, however, that the hardness of these last examples listed above remains purely conjectural and has yet to be more precisely assessed.
assertions.certainty_reason: Sec. VI i) states the limit of the physical relevance claim.

papers.title_in_file: Quantum Adversarial Learning for Kernel Methods
papers.what_it_is: A simulation study, with one single-sample hardware run, of evasion attacks on quantum-kernel SVM classifiers and adversarial training as a defence.

assertions.value: The authors report that a trained quantum-kernel SVM classifier was deceived by every adversarial example they generated, so all perturbed examples in the extended test set were wrongly classified.
quotes: We generate 50 adversarial images for both large and compact embeddings and randomly distribute them using a stratified approach into two sets

As expected, checking the behaviour of the trained QSVM classifier on the extended test dataset reveals a decrease of the performance. As detailed in Table. IV all the perturbed examples are wrongly classified.
assertions.certainty_reason: The attacks are white-box and deceive the classifier by construction (Sec. 4.2); one dataset in simulation.
assertions.reader_inference: The examples succeed by construction, so the result shows the attack procedure works, not an attack success rate.

assertions.value: The authors report a significant increase in performance after adversarial training on the same dataset, with the exact accuracies given in Table V, and conclude that adversarial training is effective for QSVM classifiers robust to evasion attacks.
quotes: After adversarial training with both models, we observe a significant increase of the performance, as detailed in Table. V.
Looking at these numerical results we can affirm that the adversarial training technique is effective for the development of QSVM classifiers robust to evasion attacks.
assertions.certainty_reason: The accuracy figures are in Table V only; the test set holds adversarial samples made against the pre-training model.
assertions.reader_inference: The test attacks were made against the earlier model, not against the retrained one, so robustness to new attacks is not shown by this table.

assertions.value: The authors state that, because of limited resources, the real-hardware experiment predicted the label of one sample only.
quotes: Because of the limitations we had on the resources available, we leveraged the quantum hardware to predict the label of one sample only.
assertions.certainty_reason: Sec. 4.3 states the scope of the hardware run.

assertions.value: The authors state that for complex embeddings the robustness of adversarial training in the kernel concentration regime is less clear and needs further studies.
quotes: the robustness of adversarial training in such regime is less clear and needs further studies.
assertions.certainty_reason: Sec. 5 states the open question.

papers.title_in_file: Training Variational Quantum Circuits Using Particle Swarm Optimization
papers.what_it_is: A short simulation study that trains the full structure of variational quantum circuits with particle swarm optimization and compares it with Adam on MedMNIST binary tasks.

assertions.value: The authors report that PSO-trained circuits reached validation accuracy similar to or better than Adam on a predefined circuit, except for pneumonia and organS, with a similar pattern on the test set, using fewer gates.
quotes: Table 1 shows the accuracy on the validation set, where PSO can achieve similar or better results, except for pneumonia and organS.
showing better performance than classical gradient descent with fewer gates.
assertions.certainty_reason: Tables 1 and 2 on binary MedMNIST tasks; one run per setting is reported.
assertions.reader_inference: No variance or repeated runs are reported, and the abstract motivation (barren plateaus) is not measured in the paper.

assertions.value: The authors state that PSO used 50 particles with 40 or 80 trainable parameters, against Adam on an 8-qubit circuit with 32 gates and 16 parameters, and that only binary tasks were considered.
quotes: the algorithm has 50 particles and has been tested with 40 and 80 dimensions, representing trainable parameters.
A VQC with 8 qubits was used, consisting of two layers of Ry rotations and CNOT gates arranged in a circular topology (32 gates and 16 parameters).
Only binary tasks were considered by selecting the first two classes
assertions.certainty_reason: Sec. 3 states the experimental setup and its scope.

assertions.value: The authors report that on the breast dataset Adam reached similar test accuracy but predicted only a single class, indicating it failed to learn meaningful patterns, while the PSO circuits began to learn both classes.
quotes: Although Adam achieved similar test accuracy, it predicts only a single class, indicating that it failed to learn meaningful patterns.
assertions.certainty_reason: One dataset, Table 3.

assertions.value: The authors report that on Rigetti and IQM devices with 1024 shots and a subset of 100 organA test samples, the PSO circuit matched its simulated accuracy, and state that multiclass classification and more complex circuits are left for future work.
quotes: Table 4 presents the results obtained on Rigetti Ankaa-3 and IQM Garnet devices using 1024 shots and a subset of 100 samples from the organ
The presence of noise does not impact the performance of the VQC optimized by PSO, which achieves results comparable to those in the ideal (noise-free) scenario.
more challenging tasks, such as multiclass classification, will be addressed.
assertions.certainty_reason: Table 4: one dataset, 100 samples; the accuracy figure is in the table.
assertions.reader_inference: One circuit on one dataset subset does not support a general statement about noise.

papers.title_in_file: Variational Quantum Algorithms for Chemical Simulation and Drug Discovery
papers.what_it_is: A simulation and small-hardware benchmark of VQE and QAOA variants on the Qiskit Nature protein-folding model, compared with AlphaFold.

assertions.value: The authors report that over 512 predictions on the QASM simulator, QAOA converged to the lowest energy state less than 2% of the time, VQE 30% of the time and CVaR VQE 99% of the time, and that the VQE and CVaR VQE top predictions fold back onto themselves, which is forbidden.
quotes: The prediction was made 512 times, the algorithm converged to the lowest energy state less than 2% of the time.
The prediction was made 512 times, the algorithm converged to the lowest energy state 30% of the time.
The prediction was made 512 times, the algorithm converged to the lowest energy state 99% of the time.
assertions.certainty_reason: Figure captions on a single peptide model.

assertions.value: The authors report an RMSD of 4.795 between the AlphaFold prediction, reduced to a bead model, and their top VQE prediction, and conclude that there are significant deviations requiring improvement of the Qiskit Nature model.
quotes: RMSD value of 4.795
find that there are significant deviations which require that the Qiskit Nature model be improved.
assertions.certainty_reason: Single comparison for one peptide.
assertions.reader_inference: The comparison is between a lattice bead model and a reduced AlphaFold structure, so the RMSD mixes model differences with algorithm quality.

assertions.value: The authors state that the reliability of the model is quite low, that a probable cause is a small energy difference between structures, and that the chain folds onto itself on multiple occasions.
quotes: The reliability of the model is quite low, a probable cause might be that the energy difference between different structures is not substantial.
A pressing problem with the current model is that chain folds onto itself on multiple occasions.
assertions.certainty_reason: Sec. V states the limits of the model.

assertions.value: The authors state that the protein Hamiltonian maps to 120 qubits and was reduced to 17 qubits with the side chain, and to 6 qubits without it.
quotes: the problem is mapped to 120 qubits but it has been optimized to 17 qubits. Similarly, it has been optimized to 6 qubits in the case without a chain.
assertions.certainty_reason: Sec. V states the paper's own problem sizes.

papers.title_in_file: Quantum vs. Classical Machine Learning Algorithms for Software Defect Prediction: Challenges and Opportunities
papers.what_it_is: An empirical comparison of three Qiskit QML algorithms and five classical algorithms on 20 software defect datasets, run on simulators.

assertions.value: The authors report that QSVC achieved the highest F1 score in 13 out of 20 datasets, with RF, GBC, PQSVC, VQC and SVC leading in 6, 5, 2, 1 and 1 datasets respectively.
quotes: achieving the highest F1 score in 13 out of 20 datasets. In contrast, the RF, GBC, PQSVC, VQC, and SVC algorithms lead in 6, 5, 2, 1, and 1 datasets, respectively
assertions.certainty_reason: Table III; simulator runs on datasets truncated to a small size.
assertions.reader_inference: The lead counts sum to 28 against 20 datasets, so ties or a counting rule are unstated; data were truncated and reduced to 15 features and 8 qubits, which limits comparison with classical models on full data.

assertions.value: The authors report that with 8 qubits and 15 features the largest dataset of 682 instances took more than 100 hours for QSVC on a simulator, and that datasets above 15 features often made QML algorithms fail to give meaningful results.
quotes: Our investigation concluded when we reached a configuration of (8 qubits, 15 feature values), which successfully produced outputs for all subject systems.
the processing time for the largest dataset (Camel in Table II), consisting of 682 data instances, exceeded 100 hours
assertions.certainty_reason: Reported run times on one server using simulators.

assertions.value: The authors state that the study used quantum simulators rather than real hardware and that further validation on actual quantum hardware is necessary to confirm the generalizability of the findings.
quotes: The primary threat to the internal validity of our study arises from the use of quantum simulators rather than real quantum hardware.
further validation on actual quantum hardware is necessary to confirm the generalizability of our findings.
assertions.certainty_reason: Sec. V Threats to Validity states the limit.

assertions.value: The authors report that on precision the classical GBC, RF and SVC outperformed all other QML and CML algorithms, and that QML algorithms showed more false positives.
quotes: Considering Precision, CML algorithms, GBC, RF, and SVC, outperform all the other QML and CML algorithms.
While considering precision, inferior performance of QML algorithms depicts more number of false positives compared to the CML algorithms.
assertions.certainty_reason: Averages across 20 datasets, Fig. 3.
assertions.reader_inference: This tempers the conclusion that QML gives better results on limited-size datasets.

papers.title_in_file: Quantum data learning for quantum simulations in high-energy physics
papers.what_it_is: A noiseless-simulation study applying quantum convolutional neural networks to quantum data from lattice gauge theory and parton shower models.

assertions.value: The authors report, from numerical simulation, that a quantum convolutional neural network ansatz recognized quantum phases of ground states in the Schwinger model and (de)confinement phases from time-evolved states in a gauge theory, and extracted fermion flavor and coupling constants in a parton shower simulation.
quotes: We make use of an ansatz based on quantum convolutional neural networks and numerically show that it is capable of recognizing quantum phases of ground states in the Schwinger model
Our results demonstrated non-trivial learning capabilities and a good generalization behavior for the QCNN method
assertions.certainty_reason: Numerical results in Secs. III to V; noiseless simulation.

assertions.value: The authors state that all results are obtained from noiseless numerical simulations using exact statevectors and unitary operations, and that a practical advantage over classical methods in learning tasks is yet to be demonstrated.
quotes: All results presented in this work are obtained from noise-
less numerical simulations, manipulating exact
the possibility of achieving concrete advantages over classical counterparts in practical learning tasks is yet to be demonstrated.
assertions.certainty_reason: Sec. II states the simulation scope; the abstract states the open advantage question.

assertions.value: The authors report that, in the setup with an unknown flavor-dependent modification to the parton shower process, the QCNN ansatz achieved superior flavor classification performance compared to a more generic hardware-efficient ansatz.
quotes: in the setup where some unknown flavor-dependent modification was made to the PS process, it achieved superior performances in flavor classification compared to a more generic hardware-efficient ansatz.
assertions.certainty_reason: Sec. V results on simulated data.

assertions.value: The authors state that a comparison with classical machine learning approaches, aimed at identifying conditions for practical quantum advantage, is a natural continuation, and that direct prediction of g12 values on non-overlapping training values gave much worse accuracy.
quotes: A comparison of the two approaches, aimed at identifying the proper conditions to achieve a practical quantum advantage, would represent a natural continuation of our line of research.

the direct prediction of g12 values was also investigated on a test dataset with nonoverlapping g12 values in the training dataset, and in this case the accuracy was much worse than for the case of predicting g1 values in Fig. 5.
assertions.certainty_reason: Sec. VI states these limits.
